newsitem.title: UK: Britain gives Dominion's East Midlands bid go-ahead.
newsitem.headline: Britain gives Dominion's East Midlands bid go-ahead.

text.p: U.S. utilities continued their multibillion-dollar takeover siege of British regional electric companies Wednesday as a new deal was announced and Britain's government approved another.
New Orleans-based Entergy Corp. agreed to buy London Electricity, which supplies power to Britain's political and financial capital, for 1.267 billion pounds ($2.11 billion).
The government, meanwhile, approved the 1.29 billion-pound ($2.15 billion) takeover of East Midlands Electricity by Richmond, Va.-based Dominion Resources Inc.
The deals leave only two independent regional electric utilities in Britain of the 12 cash-rich companies that emerged from privatisation in 1990: Yorkshire Electricity and Southern Electric.
Yorkshire, which could carry a price tag of about 1.4 billion pounds ($2.33 billion), appears to be the more vulnerable of the two, analysts said.
If the latest deals go through -- including Omaha, Neb.-based CalEnergy Co. Inc.'s 782 million-pound ($1.3 billion) hostile bid for Northern Electric Plc -- six of the 12 will be U.S.-owned.
The agreement between Entergy and London Electricity, which supplies power to Britain's capital, came after talks that were called off in November.
London's chairman, Sir Bob Reid, "did an excellent job of extracting a generous price out of us," Entergy Chairman Ed Lupberger said in an interview.
The bid values London stock at 705 pence ($11.74) each, and London shareholders will retain the right to receive a 14.3-pence (24 cents) interim dividend, the companies said in a joint statement.
Lupberger declined to comment on the process leading up to the bid.

The two companies conceded in a statement in November that talks between them broke down after the Wall Street Journal Europe reported Entergy was considering a 1.2 billion pound ($1.99 billion) bid at around 700 pence ($11.66) per share.
In the Dominion Resources-East Midlands merger, Trade and Industry Minister Ian Lang said he decided not to refer the deal to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission for further consideration.
The deal was announced Nov. 13 after weeks of speculation.
Lang said his decision was in line with his general approach to mergers involving regional electric companies.
Doubts among some investors that the deal would win approval had kept a lid on the price of East Midlands stock.
But after Lang's announcement Friday clearing the CalEnergy bid for Northern Electric analysts said the Dominion-East Midlands deal was also likely to get the go-ahead.
In addition to competition issues, Lang said he had examined other public interest issues raised by Dominion's bid.

He said the Dominion Resources subsidiary involved in the transaction had given assurances to address regulators' concerns, including ensuring sufficient resources for East Midlands to continue to meet its obligations and measures to ensure financial independence for East Midlands.
Dominion said Monday that it had won acceptances for shares representing 32.8 percent of East Midlands.
American utilities, faced with slow growth and deregulation in their home markets, have been looking for acquisitions overseas.
"The U.S. is uninteresting and these companies have money to spend, that's the long and short of it," said one analyst who asked not to be identified.
